items.stem: A VP sponsoring a drafting tool for renewal letters plans to judge success from user feedback after launch, without recording current handling time or turnaround days for the 40,000 letters processed yearly. What should the architect do first?

opts.t: Build the drafting tool now and gather user feedback after launch to see whether it helped.
Deploy the tool with usage dashboards and derive the baseline retrospectively from those logs.
Measure current handling time and turnaround days for renewal letters before committing to a design.
Skip baseline measurement and frame the rollout as a transformation success story instead.

items.whyRight: Turnaround and handling time are the units the business case will be judged in; without a recorded before, the launch cannot be shown to have helped even if it works, which is the exact failure the misconception invites.

whyWrong.A: Waiting for after-launch feedback captures no before figure; the improvement claim has nothing recorded to compare against.
whyWrong.B: Deployed system logs reconstruct downstream a measurement the pre-project step could have captured cleanly beforehand.
whyWrong.D: Renewal-letter drafting already exists as a human task, so an efficiency baseline applies; transformation framing is for capabilities that did not exist before.

items.t1Clause: for the 40,000 letters processed yearly (an already-existing, human-done process)

items.stem: A support system's citations became inaccurate after last week's document refresh; compliance relies on them for a regulated audit trail across 30,000 monthly tickets. Model version and prompt are unchanged. Which fix should the architect apply?

opts.t: Re-index and refresh the retrieval layer's embeddings so lookups reflect the newly published source documents.
Replace the underlying model with a more capable one, since it is the newest available version.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to double-check each citation before responding.
Capture the mismatched citations and route them into the evaluation set for future model tuning.

items.whyRight: The citations broke immediately after the document refresh while the model and prompt held steady, which locates the fault in the retrieval layer; re-indexing against the refreshed sources fixes the cause instead of the model or the prompt.

whyWrong.B: The model version did not change, so the model is not the failure point; replacing it does not touch the stale retrieval index causing the mismatch.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction asks the model to try harder; it cannot correct citations pointing at documents the index has not updated to reflect.
whyWrong.D: Model version and prompt are stated as unchanged, so this is not a tuning problem; routing it to the eval set delays the fix without touching the index.

items.t1Clause: the citations went wrong immediately after a scheduled document refresh
items.factAnswerRaw: Route the signal to the retrieval/indexing layer

items.stem: A vendor-onboarding pipeline runs the same five checks for every submission across 2,000 vendors monthly, but one step reconciles an uploaded document set whose count, order, and naming vary unpredictably per vendor. How should that step be designed?

opts.t: Keep the other four checks fixed; give the reconciliation step an agent planning its approach per submission.
Extend the fixed pipeline's reconciliation logic to cover the most common document layouts seen so far.
Replace the entire five-check pipeline with one agent planning every step for each submission.
Route any submission with more than three documents to a human reviewer instead.

items.whyRight: Four of the five checks are enumerable and belong in a fixed pipeline, but the reconciliation step's shape is genuinely unlistable per vendor; giving only that step an agent buys adaptive planning where it is actually needed, and nowhere else.

whyWrong.B: Extending the template to the most common layouts covers the majority silently, but drops the vendors whose document sets do not match any listed shape.
whyWrong.C: The other four checks are enumerable and fixed by requirement; replacing them with agentic planning buys nondeterminism the stated task never asked for.
whyWrong.D: Sending the variable cases to a human reviewer abandons the automation requirement for exactly the population that needed a working design.

items.t1Clause: whose count, order, and naming vary unpredictably per vendor
items.factAnswerRaw: Keep the other four checks fixed; give the reconciliation step an agent planning its approach per submission.

items.stem: An expense agent extracts a vendor name from each receipt, and a downstream step needs that name to look up the approved spending category, across 50,000 monthly submissions with a 24-hour reimbursement commitment. How should the steps be orchestrated?

opts.t: Keep both steps in the current order but switch to a faster underlying model to shorten wall-clock time.
Dispatch both steps together from a single coordinator turn, since that is how independent subtasks are parallelized.
Chain the steps sequentially so the lookup runs only after extraction returns the vendor name.
Let both steps run as issued and add a monitoring check flagging any lookup with an empty vendor name.

items.whyRight: The lookup step cannot begin until it has the vendor name the extraction step produces, which is a real data dependency; sequential chaining is required, and issuing both in one turn would send an empty value downstream.

whyWrong.A: A faster model shortens each call but does not remove the dependency; the lookup still cannot run before extraction has returned a name.
whyWrong.B: Single-turn dispatch parallelizes independent subtasks; here the lookup depends on the extraction's output, so issuing both together sends the lookup an empty value.
whyWrong.D: Monitoring an empty vendor name after the call detects the failure but does not prevent it; the sequencing itself must guarantee the value exists first.

items.t1Clause: a downstream step needs that name to look up the approved spending category

items.stem: A claims-intake team must meet a stated six-hour acknowledgment SLA and hold cost per claim within a set ceiling as intake volume triples during renewal season. Which architecture should the team adopt?

opts.t: Route every claim through confidence-tier logic to the smallest model that clears the bar, minimizing cost per claim.
Keep the current pipeline and add an automated alert that escalates whenever the acknowledgment SLA is breached.
Parallelize the independent intake checks to meet the SLA, applying confidence-tier routing only to hold cost within the ceiling.
Replace the pipeline with a fully autonomous agent that decides each claim's routing case by case.

items.whyRight: The SLA is a stated commitment that filters designs before comparison; parallelizing removes the serial depth causing the miss, and confidence-tier routing keeps cost inside the ceiling. The pure cost-tier design meets cost alone and still breaches the commitment, which is the trap this facet targets.

whyWrong.A: Confidence-tier routing to the smallest model lowers average cost, but it does nothing about the serial depth causing the SLA miss under peak volume.
whyWrong.B: An alert on a breach reports the failure after it happens; it does not remove the serial dependency that causes the SLA to be missed.
whyWrong.D: A case-by-case agent's cost is a distribution, not a point; its tail can breach both the cost ceiling and the acknowledgment SLA under tripled volume.

items.t1Clause: must meet a stated six-hour acknowledgment SLA
items.factAnswerRaw: Pick the one meeting the commitment
